title: ROMEO AND JULIET
credit: Written by William Shakespeare Adapted from The Folger Edition edited by Barbara A. Mowat and Paul Werstine

scenes.title: Prologue

lines: Two households, both alike in dignity
(In fair Verona, where we lay our scene),
From ancient grudge break to new mutiny,
Where civil blood makes civil hands unclean.
From forth the fatal loins of these two foes
A pair of star-crossed lovers take their life;
Whose misadventured piteous overthrows
Doth with their death bury their parents’ strife.
items.plain: In the city of Verona, two important families have an old feud that keeps breaking into new fights. A boy and a girl from these enemy families fall in love and die, and only their deaths end their parents' fighting.
items.why: The play is about to begin. You tell the audience what story they are going to see.

scenes.summary: The Chorus tells the audience the whole story before it starts. Two feuding families, two young lovers, and a sad ending.

wants.chorus: To make the audience lean in and listen to the story you are about to tell.

scenes.title: The Street Fight

items.text: Enter SAMPSON, GREGORY, ABRAHAM and another MONTAGUE.

lines: Draw thy tool. Here comes of the house of Montagues. I will frown as I pass by, and let them take it as they list.
items.plain: Get your sword out. Here come some Montagues. I'll scowl at them as I walk by, and they can take it however they like.
items.why: You spot Montague servants coming. You want to look tough and stir up trouble.

lines: Nay, as they dare. I will bite my thumb at them, which is disgrace to them if they bear it.
items.plain: Or however they dare. I'll bite my thumb at them. That's a big insult if they put up with it.
items.why: Gregory wants to stare them down. You want to go one better and insult them.

lines: Do you bite your thumb at us, sir?
items.plain: Are you biting your thumb at us?
items.why: You see a Capulet biting his thumb. You demand to know if it's aimed at you.

lines: I do bite my thumb, sir.
items.plain: I am biting my thumb.
items.why: Abraham challenges you. You admit to the thumb but dodge the question.

lines: Do you bite your thumb at us, sir?
items.plain: Are you biting your thumb at us?
items.why: He dodged your question. You ask again, harder.

lines: No, sir, I do not bite my thumb at you, sir, but I bite my thumb, sir.
items.plain: No, I'm not biting my thumb at you. But I am biting my thumb.
items.why: He asks again. You back off just enough to stay out of trouble, but keep the insult.

lines: Do you quarrel, sir?
items.plain: Are you trying to start a fight?
items.why: The insult is hanging in the air. You push them to say they want a fight.

lines: Quarrel, sir? No, sir.
items.plain: A fight? No.
items.why: They ask if you want a fight. You deny it, but you don't back away.

lines: But if you do, sir, I am for you. I serve as good a man as you.
items.plain: Because if you are, I'm ready. My master is just as good as yours.
items.why: He says no. You make sure he knows you're ready anyway, and brag about your master.

lines: No better.
items.plain: But not better.
items.why: He brags his master is as good as yours. You won't let him claim more.

lines: Part, fools!
Put up your swords. You know not what you do.
items.plain: Break it up, you fools! Put your swords away. You don't know what you're doing.
items.why: You walk in on servants fighting. You want to stop it before someone gets hurt.

lines: What, are thou drawn among these heartless hinds?
Turn thee, Benvolio; look up thy death.
items.plain: What, you've drawn your sword against these cowardly servants? Turn around, Benvolio, and face your death.
items.why: You see Benvolio with his sword out. You want a real fight with a real Montague.

lines: I do but keep the peace. Put up thy sword!
items.plain: I'm only trying to keep the peace. Put your sword away!
items.why: Tybalt threatens you. You try to calm him and get his help stopping the fight.

lines: What, drawn and talk of peace? I hate the word
As I hate hell, all Montague’s, and thee.
Have at thee, coward!
items.plain: Your sword is out and you talk about peace? I hate that word, the way I hate hell, every Montague, and you. Fight me, coward!
items.why: Benvolio says "peace." That word disgusts you, so you attack.

items.text: They all fight. Enter PRINCE, LORD & LADY CAPULET, LADY MONTAGUE.

lines: Rebellious subjects, enemies to peace,
Throw your mistempered weapons to the ground
And hear the sentence of your mov`ed prince.
Three civil brawls bred of an airy word
By thee, old Capulet, and Montague,
Have thrice disturbed the quiet of our streets.
If you ever you disturb our streets again,
Your lives shall pay the forfeit of the peace.
Once more, on pain of death, all men depart.
items.plain: You troublemakers, enemies of peace, throw down your weapons and listen to your angry prince. Three times now, fights between the Capulets and Montagues have disturbed our streets. If you ever do it again, you will pay with your lives. Now everyone leave, or you'll be put to death.
items.why: Your city is brawling again. You stop it and warn that the next fight means death.

items.text: Exeunt all EXCEPT LADY MONTAGUE and BENVOLIO.

lines: O, where is Romeo? Saw you him today?
Right glad I am he was not at this fray.
items.plain: Where is Romeo? Have you seen him today? I'm so glad he wasn't in this fight.
items.why: The fight is over. You're worried about your son and relieved he wasn't in it.

lines: See where he comes. So please you, step aside.
I’ll know his grievance or be much denied.
items.plain: Look, here he comes. Please step aside. I'll find out what's bothering him, or at least try hard.
items.why: She asks about Romeo, and you see him coming. You offer to find out what's wrong.

lines: I would thou wert so happy by thy stay
To hear the true shrift.—Let’s away.
items.plain: I hope you're lucky enough to hear the truth from him. Let's go.
items.why: Benvolio offers to talk to Romeo. You wish him luck and leave them alone.

lines: Good morrow, cousin.
items.plain: Good morning, cousin.
items.why: Romeo walks up looking miserable. You greet him cheerfully.

lines: Is the day so young?
items.plain: Is it still that early?
items.why: Benvolio says good morning. You can't believe the day is still so young.

lines: But new struck nine.
items.plain: It's only just nine o'clock.
items.why: Romeo thinks it's later. You tell him the time.

lines: Ay me, sad hours seem long.
items.plain: Oh dear. Sad hours feel so long.
items.why: It's only nine. Time drags because you're sad.

lines: What sadness lengthens Romeo’s hours?
items.plain: What sadness is making your hours feel long?
items.why: He says sad hours are long. You want to know what the sadness is.

lines: Not having that which, having, makes them short.
items.plain: Not having the thing that would make them feel short.
items.why: He asks what's making you sad. You answer with a riddle.

lines: In love?
items.plain: Are you in love?
items.why: His riddle sounds like love. You guess.

lines: Out—
items.plain: Out.
items.why: He guesses "in love." You start to correct him.

lines: Of love?
items.plain: Out of love?
items.why: He says "out." You try to finish his thought.

lines: Out of her favor where I am in love.
items.plain: The girl I love doesn't love me back.
items.why: He's almost right. You explain: she doesn't love you back.

lines: Tell me in sadness, who is it that you love?
items.plain: Tell me seriously, who is it you love?
items.why: So it is a girl. You want her name.

lines: What, shall I groan and tell thee?
items.plain: What, should I groan and tell you?
items.why: He asks who. You tease instead of telling.

lines: Groan? Why, no. But sadly tell me who.
items.plain: Groan? No. But tell me seriously who it is.
items.why: He's being dramatic. You ask again, seriously.

lines: In sadness, cousin, I do love a woman.
items.plain: Seriously, cousin, I love a woman.
items.why: He wants a serious answer. You give a silly, obvious one.

lines: I aimed so near when I supposed you loved.
items.plain: I guessed that much when I figured you were in love.
items.why: "A woman." You already knew that much, and say so.

lines: A right good marksman! And she’s fair I love.
She hath forsworn to love, and in that vow
Do I live dead, that live to tell it now.
items.plain: Good guess! And she's beautiful. But she has sworn never to fall in love, and that promise makes me feel like the living dead.
items.why: He says he guessed it. You praise his aim and explain she has sworn off love.

lines: Be ruled by me. Forget to think of her.
items.plain: Take my advice. Stop thinking about her.
items.why: He's stuck on a girl who won't love him. You give him advice.

lines: O, teach me how I should forget to think!
items.plain: Then teach me how to stop thinking!
items.why: He says forget her. You don't know how.

lines: By giving liberty unto thine eyes.
Examine other beauties.
items.plain: Let your eyes wander. Look at other pretty girls.
items.why: He asks how to forget. You have the answer: look at other girls.

lines: Show me a mistress that is passing fair;
Farewell. Thou canst not teach me to forget.
items.plain: Show me any beautiful girl and she'll only remind me of the one I love. Goodbye. You can't teach me to forget.
items.why: He says look at others. You're sure that would only remind you of her, so you give up and leave.

lines: I’ll pay that doctrine or else die in debt.
items.plain: I'll teach you that lesson, or die trying.
items.why: Romeo says you can't teach him to forget. You promise you will.

scenes.summary: Servants from the two families start a street fight. The Prince stops it and threatens death for the next one. Then Benvolio finds Romeo sad over a girl who does not love him.

wants.gregory: To look tough in front of the Montagues and stir up trouble.
wants.sampson: To insult the Montagues without getting blamed for starting the fight.
wants.abraham: To stand up for the Montagues and not let an insult pass.
wants.benvolio: To stop the fighting, then to find out what is wrong with Romeo and cheer him up.
wants.tybalt: To fight a Montague. Any Montague.
wants.prince: To end the brawling in your city for good.
wants.lady-montague: To find out where your son is and what is troubling him.
wants.romeo: To be left alone with your heartbreak. Rosaline does not love you back.

scenes.title: The Invitation

lines: Now, my lord, what say you to my suit?
items.plain: So, my lord, what do you say to my request to marry Juliet?
items.why: You've asked Lord Capulet to let you marry Juliet. You want his answer.

lines: Woo her, gentle Paris, get her heart;
My will to her consent is but a part.
And, she agreed, within her scope of choice
Lies my consent and fair according voice.
This night I hold an old accustomed feast,
Whereto I have invited many a guest.
Come go with me.
[to Peter] Go, sirrah, trudge about
Through fair Verona, find those persons out
Whose names are written there, and to them say
My house and welcome on their pleasure stay.
items.plain: Win her heart, Paris. My permission is only part of it. If she chooses you, I'll agree. Tonight I'm throwing my yearly party with lots of guests. Come with me. [to Peter] You, go all over Verona, find the people on this list, and tell them they're welcome at my house.
items.why: Paris wants your daughter. You tell him to win her heart first, invite him to your party, then send Peter off with the guest list.

lines: Find them out whose names are written here! I am sent to find those persons whose names are here writ, and can never find what names the writing person hath here writ. I must to the learned. In good time!
items.plain: Find the people whose names are written here! But I can't read what's written here. I'll have to find someone who can read. Ah, just in time!
items.why: Your master hands you a list and leaves. You panic, because you can't read.

lines: God gi’ good e’en. I pray sir, can you read?
items.plain: Good evening. Excuse me, sir, can you read?
items.why: Two gentlemen walk up. You need someone who can read.

lines: Ay, if I know the letters and the language.
items.plain: Yes, if I know the letters and the language.
items.why: The servant asks if you can read. You joke with him.

lines: You say honestly. Rest you merry.
items.plain: That's an honest answer. Have a nice day.
items.why: His answer sounds like "no." You give up politely and start to go.

lines: Stay, fellow. I can read.
Signior Martino and his wife and daughters,
Mercutio and his brother Valentine
My fair niece Rosaline,
Signior Valentino and his cousin, Tybalt.
A fair assembly. Whither should they come?
items.plain: Wait, I can read. [He reads the guest list.] That's a fine group of people. Where are they supposed to go?
items.why: He's leaving. You stop him and read the list. You wonder where all these guests are going.

lines: Up.
items.plain: Up.
items.why: He asks where the guests should come. You point.

lines: Whither? To supper?
items.plain: Where? To dinner?
items.why: "Up" tells you nothing. You ask again.

lines: To our house.
items.plain: To our house.
items.why: He asks if it's for supper. You say where.

lines: Whose house?
items.plain: Whose house?
items.why: "Our house." You still don't know whose.

lines: My master’s.
items.plain: My master's.
items.why: He asks whose house. You answer exactly that and no more.

lines: Indeed, I should have asked thee that before.
items.plain: Right, I should have asked you that first.
items.why: He's no help. You realise you asked the wrong question.

lines: Now I’ll tell you without asking. My master is the great rich Capulet, and if you be not of the house of Montagues, I pray come and crush a cup of wine. Rest you merry.
items.plain: I'll tell you without your asking. My master is the great, rich Capulet. As long as you're not Montagues, come and have a drink with us. Have a nice day.
items.why: He's stopped asking, so now you tell him everything and invite him, as long as he's no Montague.

lines: At this same ancient feast of Capulet’s
Sups the fair Rosaline who thou so loves,
With all the admire`d beauties of Verona.
Go thither, and with unattainted eye
Compare her face to one that I shall show,
And I will make thee think thy swan a crow.
items.plain: Rosaline, the girl you love, will be at this Capulet party, along with every beauty in Verona. Go there, look with fresh eyes, and compare her with a girl I'll show you. I'll make you think your swan is a crow.
items.why: Rosaline is on that guest list. You see your chance to show Romeo prettier girls.

lines: I’ll go along, no such sight to be shown
But to rejoice in splendor of mine own.
items.plain: I'll go, but not to look at other girls. I'll go to enjoy seeing my own love.
items.why: Benvolio says another girl will outshine her. You'll go, but only to look at Rosaline.

scenes.summary: Paris asks Lord Capulet for permission to marry Juliet. Capulet sends Peter out with a party guest list, but Peter cannot read. He asks Romeo for help, and Romeo learns about the party.

wants.paris: To get Lord Capulet to say yes to marrying Juliet.
wants.lord-capulet: To be a good host and a careful father. Paris should win Juliet's heart first.
wants.peter: To find someone who can read the list before you get in trouble.
wants.romeo: To see Rosaline, who will be at the party.
wants.benvolio: To get Romeo to the party so he will notice other girls.

scenes.title: Juliet and Her Mother

lines: Nurse, where’s my daughter? Call her forth to me.
items.plain: Nurse, where is my daughter? Call her for me.
items.why: You have important news for your daughter. You tell the Nurse to fetch her.

lines: What, lamb? What, ladybird? God forbid. Where’s this girl? What, Juliet!
items.plain: Lamb! Ladybird! Goodness, where is that girl? Juliet!
items.why: Lady Capulet wants Juliet. You call for her.

lines: Madam, I am here. What is your will?
items.plain: I'm here, Mother. What do you want?
items.why: You hear your name called. You come and ask what your mother wants.

lines: This is the matter—Nurse, give leave awhile.
We must talk in secret.—Nurse, come back again.
Thou knowest my daughter’s of a pretty age.
items.plain: Here's the thing. Nurse, leave us alone a moment. We need to talk in private. No, Nurse, come back. You know my daughter is at a good age.
items.why: Juliet is here. You want privacy, then change your mind and keep the Nurse.

lines: Faith, I can tell her age unto an hour.
Thou wast the prettiest babe that e’er I nursed
An I might live to see thee married once,
I have my wish.
items.plain: I can tell you her age to the hour. You were the prettiest baby I ever cared for. If I live to see you married, I'll have my wish.
items.why: Lady Capulet mentions Juliet's age. You know it better than anyone and can't help chatting.

lines: Marry, that “marry” is the very theme
I came to talk of.— Tell me, daughter Juliet
How stands your disposition to be married?
items.plain: Marriage is exactly what I came to talk about. Tell me, Juliet, how do you feel about getting married?
items.why: The Nurse said "married." That's exactly your subject, so you ask Juliet.

lines: It is an honor that I dream not of.
items.plain: It's an honor I haven't even dreamed about.
items.why: Your mother asks how you feel about marriage. You've never thought about it.

lines: The valiant Paris seeks you for his love. Verona’s summer hath not such a flower.
items.plain: The brave Paris wants to marry you. He's the finest young man in all Verona.
items.why: Juliet hasn't thought about it. You tell her who wants her.

lines: Nay, he’s a flower, in faith, a very flower.
items.plain: Yes, he's a flower, a real flower.
items.why: She praises Paris as a flower. You eagerly agree.

lines: What say you? Can you love the gentleman?
This night you shall behold him at our feast.
Read o’er the volume of young Paris’ face,
And find delight writ there with beauty’s pen.
Speak briefly. Can you like of Paris’ love?
items.plain: What do you say? Could you love him? You'll see him at our party tonight. Study his face like a book and enjoy the beauty written there. Answer quickly: could you accept Paris's love?
items.why: You want Juliet's answer. You push her to look Paris over tonight and decide.

lines: I’ll look to like, if looking liking move.
But no more deep will I endart mine eye
Than your consent gives strength to make it fly.
items.plain: I'll look at him and see if I like him. But I won't let myself fall any further than you give me permission to.
items.why: Your mother wants a yes. You promise to look, but only as far as she allows.

lines: Madam, the guests are come, supper served up, you called, my young lady asked for, the Nurse cursed in the pantry, and everything in extremity. I must hence to wait. I beseech you, follow straight.
items.plain: Madam, the guests are here, dinner is served, people are asking for you and for Juliet, they're cursing the Nurse in the kitchen, and everything is crazy. I have to go serve. Please come right away.
items.why: The party is starting and the kitchen is in chaos. You rush in to fetch the ladies.

lines: We follow thee.
Juliet, the County stays.
items.plain: We're coming. Juliet, Count Paris is waiting.
items.why: The servant says the guests are here. You hurry Juliet along.

lines: Go, girl, seek happy nights to happy days.
items.plain: Go, girl, and find happy nights to go with your happy days.
items.why: Juliet is off to meet Paris. You send her with a happy wish.

scenes.summary: Lady Capulet tells Juliet that Paris wants to marry her. The Nurse cannot stop talking. Juliet agrees to look at Paris at the party tonight.

wants.lady-capulet: To get Juliet to agree to consider Paris.
wants.nurse: To be part of the big news and see your girl happily married.
wants.juliet: To be a good daughter without promising anything.
wants.servant-1: To get the ladies to the party right now. Everything is chaos.

scenes.title: Queen Mab

lines: Give me a torch. I am not for this ambling.
Being but heavy I will bear the light.
items.plain: Give me a torch to carry. I'm not in the mood for dancing. Since I'm feeling heavy and sad, I'll carry the light.
items.why: You're outside the party with your friends. You're too sad to dance.

lines: Nay, gentle Romeo, we must have you dance.
items.plain: No, Romeo, we have to get you dancing.
items.why: Romeo wants to stand and hold a torch. You won't allow it.

lines: Not I, believe me. You have dancing shoes
With nimble soles. I have a soul of lead
So stakes me to the ground, I cannot move.
items.plain: Not me. You have dancing shoes with light soles. My soul feels like lead. It pins me to the ground so I can't move.
items.why: Mercutio insists you dance. You explain how heavy you feel.

lines: You are a lover. Borrow Cupid’s wings
And soar them above a common bound.
items.plain: You're in love. Borrow Cupid's wings and fly high.
items.why: He says his soul is lead. You tell the lover to borrow Cupid's wings.

lines: Come, knock and enter, and no sooner in
But every man betake him to his legs.
items.plain: Come on, let's knock and go in. As soon as we're inside, everybody start dancing.
items.why: They're wasting time arguing. You want to get inside.

lines: Come, we burn daylight, ho!
items.plain: Come on, we're wasting time!
items.why: Benvolio says go in. You agree: hurry up.

lines: Nay, that’s not so.
items.plain: No, we're not.
items.why: Mercutio says you're wasting daylight. You disagree.

lines: Why may one ask?
items.plain: Why do you say that?
items.why: Romeo contradicts you. You ask why.

lines: I dreamt a dream tonight.
items.plain: I had a dream last night.
items.why: He asks why. You bring up your dream.

lines: And so did I.
items.plain: So did I.
items.why: He had a dream. You say you had one too.

lines: Well, what was yours?
items.plain: Well, what was yours?
items.why: Mercutio dreamed too. You ask what about.

lines: That dreamers often lie.
items.plain: That dreamers often lie.
items.why: He asks about your dream. You turn it into a joke.

lines: In bed asleep while they do dream things true.
items.plain: They lie in bed asleep, while they dream things that are true.
items.why: He says dreamers lie. You twist it: they lie in bed, dreaming true things.

lines: O, then I see Queen Mab hath been with you.
She is the fairies’ midwife, and she comes
In shape no bigger than an agate stone
On the forefinger of an alderman,
Drawn with a team of little atomies
Over men’s noses as they lie asleep.
And in this state she gallops night by night
Through lovers’ brains, and then they dream of love;
On courtiers’ knees, that dream on cur’sies straight;
O’er lawyers’ fingers, who straight dream on fees;
O’er ladies’ lips, who straight on kisses dream,
Which oft the angry Mab with blisters plagues
Because their breaths with sweetmeats tainted are.
This is she—
items.plain: Oh, then Queen Mab has visited you. She's the fairies' midwife, no bigger than a tiny stone on a ring. Her little team pulls her across people's noses as they sleep. She rides through lovers' brains and they dream of love, over lawyers' fingers and they dream of money, over ladies' lips and they dream of kisses. This is the fairy who...
items.why: Romeo believes in dreams. You launch into a wild story about the dream fairy, Queen Mab.

lines: Peace, peace, Mercutio, peace.
Thou talk’st of nothing.
items.plain: Quiet, Mercutio, quiet. You're talking about nothing.
items.why: Mercutio is getting carried away. You stop him.

lines: True, I talk of dreams,
Which are the children of an idle brain,
Begot of nothing but vain fantasy,
Which is as thin of substance of the air
And more inconstant than the wind.
items.plain: True. I'm talking about dreams. They come from a lazy brain and from silly imagination, which is as thin as air and changes faster than the wind.
items.why: Romeo says you talk of nothing. You agree: dreams are nothing.

lines: This wind you talk of blows us from ourselves.
Supper is done, and we shall come too late.
items.plain: All this talk of wind is blowing us off course. Dinner is over and we're going to be too late.
items.why: All this talk is making you late. You pull them back to the party.

lines: He that hath the steerage of my course
Direct my sail. On, lusty gentleman.
items.plain: Whoever is steering my life, guide me. Let's go, friends.
items.why: You have a bad feeling about tonight. You decide to trust fate and go anyway.

lines: Strike, drum!
items.plain: Beat the drum!
items.why: Romeo says "On." You give the signal to march in.

scenes.summary: Romeo, Benvolio and Mercutio are on their way to sneak into the Capulet party. Romeo is gloomy and has had a bad dream. Mercutio teases him with a wild speech about Queen Mab, the dream fairy.

wants.romeo: To hang back. You have a bad feeling about tonight.
wants.mercutio: To shake Romeo out of his mood and get him dancing.
wants.benvolio: To get everyone inside before the party is over.

scenes.title: The Capulet Party

items.text: Enter LORD CAPULET, LADY CAPULET, ROMEO, MERCUTIO, PARIS, JULIET, TYBALT, NURSE, MUSICIANS, AND SERVANTS.

lines: Welcome, gentleman. Ladies that have their toes
Unplagued with corns will walk about with you.
You are welcome!—Come, musicians, play.
A hall, a hall, give room!—And foot it, girls.—
items.plain: Welcome, gentlemen! Any lady without sore feet will dance with you. You're welcome here! Musicians, play! Make room, everyone! Dance, girls!
items.why: Your guests are arriving. You welcome them and get the dancing started.

lines: What lady’s that which doth enrich the hand
Of yonder knight?
items.plain: Who is that girl holding that knight's hand?
items.why: You see a girl across the room and can't look away. You ask who she is.

lines: I know not, sir.
items.plain: I don't know, sir.
items.why: A masked guest asks about a girl. You don't know her.

lines: O, she doth teach the torches to burn bright!
Did my heart love till now? Forswear it, sight,
For I ne’er saw true beauty till this night.
items.plain: Oh, she shines brighter than the torches! Did my heart ever love before now? My eyes say no. I never saw real beauty until tonight.
items.why: No one can name her. You're stunned by her beauty.

lines: This, by his voice, should be a Montague.
What, dares the man
Come hither covered with an antic face
To fleer and scorn at our solemnity?
Now, by the stock and honor of my kin,
To strike him dead I hold it not a sin.
items.plain: By his voice, this must be a Montague. How dare he come here wearing a mask to make fun of our party? By the honor of my family, I wouldn't call it a sin to strike him dead.
items.why: You hear a voice you know. A Montague is at your family's party, and you want to kill him.

lines: Why, how now, kinsman? Wherefore storm you so?
items.plain: What's the matter, nephew? Why are you so angry?
items.why: Your nephew is fuming. You ask why.

lines: Uncle, this is a Montague, our foe,
A villain that is hither come in spite
To scorn at our solemnity this night.
items.plain: Uncle, that's a Montague, our enemy. He's a villain who came here out of spite to mock our party.
items.why: Your uncle asks what's wrong. You point out the enemy.

lines: Young Romeo is it? Take no note of him.
It is my will, the which if thou respect,
Show a fair presence and put off these frowns,
An ill-beseeming semblance for a feast.
items.plain: It's young Romeo, is it? Leave him alone. That's what I want. If you respect me, look friendly and stop frowning. A scowl doesn't belong at a party.
items.why: It's only young Romeo. You order Tybalt to leave him alone.

lines: I’ll not endure him.
items.plain: I won't put up with him.
items.why: Your uncle says ignore him. You refuse.

lines: He shall be endured.
What, goodman boy? I say he shall. Go to.
You are a saucy boy.
Be quiet, or for shame I’ll make you quiet!
items.plain: You will put up with him. What, boy? I say you will. You are a rude boy. Be quiet, or I'll make you be quiet!
items.why: Tybalt defies you in your own house. You put him in his place.

lines: I will withdraw, but this intrusion shall
Now seeming sweet, convert to bitt’rest gall.
items.plain: I'll leave. But his barging in here may seem sweet now, and it will turn bitter later.
items.why: You're forced to back down. You leave, promising this isn't over.

lines: If I profrane with my unworthiest hand
This holy shrine, the gentle sin is this:
My lips, two blushing pilgrims, ready stand
To smooth that rough touch with a tender kiss.
items.plain: If my rough hand is not good enough to touch your holy hand, then my lips are ready, like two blushing pilgrims, to smooth that touch with a gentle kiss.
items.why: You reach her and take her hand. You ask for a kiss by calling her a saint.

lines: Good pilgrim, you do wrong your hand too much,
Which mannerly devotion shows in this;
For saints have hands that pilgrims’ hands do much,
And palm to palm is holy palmers’ kiss.
items.plain: Good pilgrim, you're too hard on your hand. Holding hands shows respect. Pilgrims touch saints' hands, and putting palm to palm is how pilgrims kiss.
items.why: A stranger takes your hand and asks for a kiss. You play along, but say hands are enough.

lines: Have not saints lips, and holy palmers too?
items.plain: Don't saints and pilgrims have lips, too?
items.why: She says hands are a pilgrim's kiss. You point out saints have lips too.

lines: Ay, pilgrim, lips that they must use in prayer.
items.plain: Yes, pilgrim, lips they're supposed to use for praying.
items.why: He mentions lips. You say lips are for praying.

lines: O then, dear saint, let lips do what hands do.
They pray: grant thou, lest faith turn to despair.
items.plain: Then, dear saint, let lips do what hands do. My lips are praying. Please say yes, or my faith will turn to despair.
items.why: She says lips pray. Then your prayer is a kiss.

lines: Saints do not move, though grant for prayers’ sake.
items.plain: Saints don't move, even when they grant a prayer.
items.why: He begs for the kiss. You hold still and let him.

lines: Then move not while my prayer’s effect I take.
[They kiss.]
Thus from my lips, by thine, my sin is purged
items.plain: Then don't move while I take what I prayed for. [They kiss.] Now your lips have taken my sin away.
items.why: She says she won't move. You kiss her.

lines: Then have my lips the sin that they have took.
items.plain: Then my lips have the sin they took from you.
items.why: He says the kiss took his sin. You tease that now you have it.

lines: Sin from thy lips? O trespass sweetly urged!
Give me thy sin.
items.plain: Sin from your lips? What a sweet thing to accuse me of! Give me my sin back.
items.why: She has your sin. You want it back, with another kiss.

lines: Madam, your mother craves a word with you!
items.plain: Miss, your mother wants a word with you!
items.why: Juliet's mother is asking for her. You interrupt.

lines: What is her mother?
items.plain: Who is her mother?
items.why: The Nurse calls her away. You ask who her mother is.

lines: Marry bachelor,
Her mother is the lady of the house.
items.plain: Well, young man, her mother is the lady of the house.
items.why: The young man asks about her mother. You tell him.

lines: Is she a Capulet?
O dear account! My life is my foe’s debt.
items.plain: She's a Capulet? What a terrible price! My life now belongs to my enemy.
items.why: The lady of the house. You realise she is a Capulet.

lines: Away, begone. The sport is at the best.
items.plain: Come on, let's go. The fun is at its best right now.
items.why: The party is at its peak. You want to leave before there's trouble.

lines: Ay, so I fear. The more is my unrest.
items.plain: Yes, I'm afraid so. That makes me even more troubled.
items.why: Benvolio says go. You're afraid your trouble has just begun.

lines: Come hither, nurse. What is yond gentleman?
items.plain: Come here, Nurse. Who is that gentleman?
items.why: He's leaving. You have to know who he is.

lines: His name is Romeo, and a Montague,
The only son of your great enemy.
items.plain: His name is Romeo, and he's a Montague. He's the only son of your great enemy.
items.why: Juliet asks his name. You tell her the bad news.

lines: My only love sprung from my only hate!
Too early seen unknown, and known too late.
Prodigious birth of love it is to me
That I must love a loath`ed enemy.
items.plain: The only boy I love is the son of the only family I hate! I saw him too early without knowing who he was, and found out too late. What a monstrous beginning for love, that I have to love my hated enemy.
items.why: He's a Montague. You're shocked that you love your enemy.

lines: Come, let’s away. The strangers all are gone.
items.plain: Come, let's go. The guests have all left.
items.why: The guests have gone. You take Juliet off to bed.

scenes.summary: At the party, Romeo sees Juliet and forgets Rosaline at once. Tybalt spots him and wants a fight, but Lord Capulet forbids it. Romeo and Juliet meet, kiss, and then each learns the other is from the enemy family.

wants.lord-capulet: To throw a wonderful party with no trouble in your house.
wants.romeo: To meet the girl you cannot stop looking at.
wants.servant-2: To do your job. You do not know who the girl is.
wants.tybalt: To throw the Montague out, or worse.
wants.juliet: To find out who this boy is and keep talking to him.
wants.nurse: To fetch Juliet for her mother and keep an eye on her.
wants.benvolio: To get Romeo out safely while things are still fun.

scenes.title: The Balcony

lines: Can I go forward when my heart is here?
items.plain: How can I walk away when my heart is here?
items.why: The party is over, but you can't leave the place where Juliet is.

lines: [offstage] Romeo, my cousin Romeo, Romeo!
[Enter BENVOLIO and MERCUTIO.]
He ran this way and leapt this orchard wall,
Call, good Mercutio.
items.plain: Romeo! Cousin Romeo! He ran this way and jumped over this orchard wall. Call him, Mercutio.
items.why: Romeo has vanished over the wall. You call for him and ask Mercutio to help.

lines: Romeo! Humors! Madman! Passion! Lover!
items.plain: Romeo! Moody! Madman! Lovesick fool!
items.why: Benvolio asks you to call. You do it by making fun of Romeo.

lines: Come, he hath hid himself among these tree.
items.plain: Come on, he's hidden himself in these trees.
items.why: No answer. You decide he's hiding.

lines: Shall we go?
items.plain: Shall we go?
items.why: Romeo won't come out. You've had enough.

lines: He jests at scars that never felt a wound.
But soft, what light through yonder window breaks?
It is the East, and Juliet is the sun.
Arise, fair sun, and kill the envious moon,
Who is already sick and pale with grief
That thou, her maid, art far more fair than she.
It is my lady. O, it is my love!
O, that she knew she were.
items.plain: It's easy to joke about scars if you've never been hurt. But wait, what light is that in the window? It is the east, and Juliet is the sun. Rise, beautiful sun, and outshine the jealous moon, which is pale with envy because you are far lovelier than she is. It's my lady. It's my love! If only she knew it.
items.why: Your friends leave, laughing at love. Then a light appears at a window: Juliet.

lines: Ay me.
items.plain: Oh, me.
items.why: You think you're alone, thinking about him. You sigh.

lines: She speaks.
items.plain: She's talking.
items.why: She sighs. You're thrilled just to hear her voice.

lines: O Romeo, Romeo, wherefore art thou Romeo?
Deny thy father and refuse thy name,
Or if thou wilt not, be but sworn my love,
And I’ll no longer be a Capulet.
items.plain: Oh Romeo, Romeo, why do you have to be Romeo? Give up your father and your name. Or if you won't, just swear you love me, and I'll stop being a Capulet.
items.why: You wish he weren't a Montague. You wish the names away.

lines: Shall I hear more, or shall I speak at this?
items.plain: Should I keep listening, or should I speak now?
items.why: She has just said she loves you. You don't know whether to speak.

lines: ’Tis but thy name that is my enemy.
Thou art thyself, though not a Montague.
What’s Montague? It is nor hand, nor foot,
Nor arm, nor face.
What’s in a name? That which we call a rose
By any other word would smell as sweet.
And, for thy name, which is no part of thee,
Take all myself.
items.plain: Only your name is my enemy. You'd still be yourself even if you weren't a Montague. What is a Montague? It isn't a hand or a foot or an arm or a face. What's in a name? A rose would smell just as sweet if we called it something else. Romeo, give up your name, which isn't part of you, and take all of me in exchange.
items.why: You keep thinking it through. It's only his name that's the problem.

lines: I take thee at thy word.
Call me but love, and I’ll be new baptized.
Henceforth I never will be Romeo.
items.plain: I'll take you at your word. Just call me your love and I'll take a new name. From now on I'll never be Romeo.
items.why: She says "take all myself." You can't stay hidden any longer.

lines: What man art thou that, thus bescreened in night,
So stumblest on my counsel?
items.plain: Who are you, hiding in the dark and listening to my private thoughts?
items.why: A voice comes out of the dark. You're startled and want to know who heard you.

lines: By a name
I know not how to tell thee who I am.
items.plain: I don't know how to tell you who I am by using a name.
items.why: She asks who you are. Your name is the one thing you can't say.

lines: Art thou not Romeo, and a Montague?
items.plain: Aren't you Romeo, and a Montague?
items.why: You know that voice. You ask if it's him.

lines: Neither, fair maid, if either thee dislike.
items.plain: Neither one, lovely girl, if you dislike either.
items.why: She asks if you're Romeo and a Montague. You'll be neither if she dislikes them.

lines: How camest thou hither?
This place is death, considering who thou art,
If any of my kinsmen find thee here.
items.plain: How did you get here? This place means death for you if any of my family find you here.
items.why: It is him. You're afraid for him: your family would kill him here.

lines: With love’s light wings did I o’erperch these walls.
items.plain: I flew over these walls on the light wings of love.
items.why: She asks how you got in. Love got you over the wall.

lines: Dost thou love me? I know wilt say “Ay,”
And I will take thy word. Yet, if thou swear’st,
Thou mayst prove false. O gentle Romeo,
If thou dost love, pronounce it faithfully.
items.plain: Do you love me? I know you'll say yes, and I'll believe you. But if you swear it, you might turn out to be lying. Oh, gentle Romeo, if you do love me, say it truthfully.
items.why: He has heard everything. You need to know if he truly loves you.

lines: Lady, by yonder blesse`d moon I swear…
items.plain: Lady, I swear by the holy moon up there...
items.why: She asks you to say it truly. You start to swear by the moon.

lines: O, swear not by the moon, th’ inconstant moon,
That monthly changes in her circled org,
Lest that thy love prove likewise variable.
items.plain: Oh, don't swear by the moon. The moon changes every month. Your love might turn out to change just as much.
items.why: He swears by the moon. You stop him, because the moon changes.

lines: What shall I swear by?
items.plain: What should I swear by?
items.why: She won't accept the moon. You ask what you should swear by.

lines: Well, do not swear. Although I joy in thee,
I have no joy in this contract tonight.
It is too rash, too unadvised, too sudden.
Sweet, good night,
This bud of love, by summer’s ripening breath,
May prove a beauteous flower when next we meet.
items.plain: Don't swear at all. I'm so happy with you, but I'm not happy about these promises tonight. It's too fast, too reckless, too sudden. Good night, my sweet. This bud of love may grow into a beautiful flower by the next time we meet.
items.why: This is all happening too fast. You try to slow down and say good night.

lines: O, wilt thou leave me so unsatisfied?
items.plain: Oh, will you leave me so unsatisfied?
items.why: She's saying good night already. You don't want it to end.

lines: What satisfaction canst thou have tonight?
I hear some noise within. Dear love, adieu.—
Anon good nurse—Sweet Montague, be true.
Stay but a little; I will come again.
items.plain: What satisfaction could you have tonight? I hear a noise inside. Goodbye, dear love. Coming, Nurse! Sweet Montague, be true. Wait just a moment. I'll come back.
items.why: He wants more. The Nurse is calling, and you have to go for a moment.

lines: O blessed, blessed night! I am afeard,
Being in night, all this is but a dream
Too flattering sweet to be substantial.
items.plain: Oh, blessed night! I'm afraid that, since it's night, this is all just a dream, too sweet to be real.
items.why: She has gone inside. You can hardly believe this is real.

lines: Three words, dear Romeo, and good night indeed.
If that thy bent of love be honorable,
Thy purpose marriage, send me word tomorrow,
By one that I’ll procure to come to thee,
Where and what time thou wilt perform the rite,
And all my fortunes at thy foot I’ll lay
And follow thee my lord throughout the world.
items.plain: Three more words, dear Romeo, and then good night for real. If your love is honorable and you mean to marry me, send me word tomorrow by a messenger I'll send to you. Tell me where and when we'll be married. Then I'll give you everything I have and follow you anywhere in the world.
items.why: You come back with a plan. If he means marriage, he should send word tomorrow.

lines: Madam.
items.plain: Miss!
items.why: Juliet should be in bed. You call for her.

lines: By and by, I come—
items.plain: I'm coming, in a moment.
items.why: The Nurse calls. You stall.

lines: So thrive my soul—
items.plain: I swear on my soul...
items.why: She has to go. You try to promise.

lines: A thousand times good night.
items.plain: A thousand times good night.
items.why: There's no time. You say good night.

lines: Romeo.
items.plain: Romeo.
items.why: You can't leave it there. You call him back.

lines: My dear.
items.plain: My dear.
items.why: She calls your name. You answer.

lines: What o’clock tomorrow
Shall I send to thee?
items.plain: What time tomorrow should I send my messenger to you?
items.why: You forgot to ask the time for tomorrow.

lines: By the hour of nine.
items.plain: At nine o'clock.
items.why: She asks what time. You tell her.

lines: I will not fail. ’Tis twenty year till then.
Goodnight, goodnight. Parting is such sweet sorrow
That I shall say “Good night” till it be morrow.
items.plain: I won't fail. It will feel like twenty years until then. Good night, good night. Saying goodbye is such sweet sadness that I'll keep saying good night until it's morning.
items.why: Nine o'clock. You promise, and you can hardly bear to say goodbye.

scenes.summary: Romeo slips away from his friends and hides in the Capulet orchard. Juliet comes to her window and, thinking she is alone, says she loves him. They talk, swear their love, and plan to marry tomorrow.

wants.romeo: To be near Juliet, to hear that she loves you, and to promise yourself to her.
wants.benvolio: To find Romeo and take him home.
wants.mercutio: To tease Romeo out of hiding, then give up and go to bed.
wants.juliet: To know that Romeo's love is real, and to turn it into a plan to marry.
wants.nurse: To get Juliet back inside and into bed.

scenes.title: Friar Lawrence's Cell

lines: The gray-eyed morn smiles on the frowning night,
Check’ring the eastern clouds with streaks of light,
And flecked darkness like a drunkard reels
From forth day’s path and Titan’s fiery wheels.
items.plain: The gray morning smiles as the frowning night leaves. Streaks of light spread across the eastern clouds, and the darkness stumbles out of the sun's path like a drunk man.
items.why: It's dawn and you're alone outside your cell. You enjoy the sunrise.

lines: Good morrow, father.
items.plain: Good morning, Father.
items.why: You've come straight from Juliet to ask a favour. You greet the Friar.

lines: Benedicite.
What early tongue so sweet saluteth me?
Young son, thy earliness doth me assure
Thou art uproused with some distemp’rature,
Or, if not so, then here I hit it right:
Our Romeo hath not been in bed tonight.
items.plain: Bless you. Who greets me so sweetly and so early? Young man, being up this early tells me something is troubling you. Or if not, then I've guessed it: our Romeo hasn't been to bed tonight.
items.why: Romeo is up very early. You guess something is wrong, or that he never went to bed.

lines: That last is true. The sweeter rest was mine.
items.plain: That last part is true. But I had a sweeter kind of rest.
items.why: He guesses you didn't sleep. You admit it, happily.

lines: God pardon sin! Wast thou with Rosaline?
items.plain: God forgive you! Were you with Rosaline?
items.why: No sleep, and so happy. You fear he was with Rosaline.

lines: With Rosaline, my ghostly father? No.
I have forgot that name and that name’s woe.
items.plain: With Rosaline, Father? No. I've forgotten that name and all the sadness that came with it.
items.why: He thinks it was Rosaline. You've forgotten her completely.

lines: That’s my good son. But where has thou been then?
items.plain: Good boy. But then where have you been?
items.why: Good, he's over Rosaline. So where was he?

lines: I have been feasting with mine enemy,
Where on a sudden one hath wounded me
That’s by me wounded.
Plainly know my heart’s dear love is set
On the fair daughter of rich Capulet
But this I pray,
That thou consent to marry us today.
items.plain: I was at a party with my enemy, where someone suddenly wounded me with love, and I wounded her back. To put it plainly, my heart is set on rich Capulet's beautiful daughter. I'm asking you to agree to marry us today.
items.why: He asks where you were. You tell him about Juliet and ask him to marry you today.

lines: Holy Saint Francis, what a change is here!
Is Rosaline, that thou didst love so dear
So soon forsaken? Young men’s love then lies
Not truly in their hearts, but in their eyes.
items.plain: Holy Saint Francis, what a change! Have you given up Rosaline, whom you loved so much, this quickly? Then young men love with their eyes, and not truly with their hearts.
items.why: Yesterday it was Rosaline, today Juliet. You're amazed at how fast he changed.

lines: I pray thee, chide me not. Her I love now
Doth grace for grace and love for love allow.
The other did not so.
items.plain: Please don't scold me. The girl I love now loves me back just as much. The other one didn't.
items.why: He's scolding you. You defend yourself: this girl loves you back.

lines: Come, young waverer, come, go with me.
In one respect I’ll thy assistant be,
For this alliance may so happy prove
To turn your household’s rancor to pure love.
items.plain: Come with me, you changeable young man. I'll help you for one reason: this marriage might just turn your families' hatred into pure love.
items.why: You see a chance: this marriage could end the feud. You agree to help.

lines: O, let us hence. I stand on sudden haste. [Exit ROMEO.]
items.plain: Oh, let's go. I'm in a great hurry.
items.why: He said yes. You want to go right now.

lines: Wisely and slow. They stumble that run fast.
items.plain: Go wisely and slowly. People who run fast trip and fall.
items.why: Romeo is rushing. You warn him to slow down.

scenes.summary: At dawn Romeo runs to Friar Lawrence and asks him to marry him to Juliet today. The Friar is shocked at how fast Romeo has changed, but agrees, hoping the marriage will end the feud.

wants.friar-lawrence: To understand what Romeo is up to, then to use this marriage to make peace between the families.
wants.romeo: To get the Friar to marry you to Juliet today.

scenes.title: The Nurse's Errand

lines: Where the devil should this Romeo be?
Came he not home tonight?
items.plain: Where the devil can Romeo be? Didn't he come home last night?
items.why: Romeo never came home last night. You ask Benvolio where he is.

lines: Not to his mother’s. I spoke with her man.
Tybalt, the kinsman to old Capulet,
Hath sent a letter to his mother’s house.
items.plain: Not to his mother's house. I talked to her servant. Tybalt, old Capulet's nephew, has sent a letter to Romeo's house.
items.why: Mercutio asks about Romeo. You share the news: Tybalt has sent a letter.

lines: A challenge, on my life.
items.plain: It's a challenge to fight, I'd bet my life on it.
items.why: A letter from Tybalt. You know what that means.

lines: Romeo will answer it.
[Enter ROMEO.]
Here comes Romeo, here comes Romeo.
items.plain: Romeo will answer it. Look, here comes Romeo.
items.why: Mercutio says it's a challenge. You're sure Romeo will answer, and then you spot him.

lines: Signior Romeo, bonjour. There’s a French salutation for your French slop. You gave us the counterfeit fairly last night.
items.plain: Sir Romeo, bonjour! There's a French hello to go with your fancy French pants. You tricked us nicely last night.
items.why: Romeo arrives at last. You tease him for sneaking off last night.

lines: Good morrow to you both. What counterfeit did I give you?
items.plain: Good morning to you both. What trick did I play on you?
items.why: Mercutio accuses you of a trick. You ask what he means.

lines: The slip, sir, the slip. Can you not conceive?
items.plain: You gave us the slip, sir. Don't you get it?
items.why: He pretends not to know. You spell it out: he gave you the slip.

lines: Pardon, good Mercutio, my business was great, and in such a case as mine a man may strain courtesy.
items.plain: I'm sorry, Mercutio. I had important business. In a situation like mine, a man can be forgiven for skipping good manners.
items.why: He's right, you ran off. You apologise and hint you had good reason.

lines: Boy.
items.plain: Boy.
items.why: You arrive with your servant to find Romeo. You call for your boy.

lines: Anon.
items.plain: Coming.
items.why: The Nurse calls. You answer.

lines: My fan, boy. God you, good morrow gentlemen. Gentleman, can any of you tell me where I may find the young Romeo?
items.plain: My fan, boy. Good morning, gentlemen. Can any of you tell me where I can find young Romeo?
items.why: You want your fan to look proper. Then you ask the young men for Romeo.

lines: I am the youngest of that name.
items.plain: I'm the youngest person with that name.
items.why: She's asking for Romeo. That's you.

lines: If you be he, sir, I desire some confidence with you.
items.plain: If you're him, sir, I'd like a private word with you.
items.why: You've found him. You want to talk in private.

lines: Romeo, will you come to your mother’s? We’ll to dinner thither.
items.plain: Romeo, are you coming to your mother's house? We're going there for lunch.
items.why: The Nurse wants Romeo alone. You're leaving for lunch and ask if he's coming.

lines: I will follow you.
items.plain: I'll catch up with you.
items.why: Mercutio asks if you're coming. You need to stay and hear from Juliet.

lines: Farewell, ancient lady. Farewell, lady, lady, lady.
items.plain: Goodbye, old lady. Goodbye, lady, lady, lady.
items.why: You're off. You can't resist mocking the Nurse on the way out.

lines: My young lady bid me inquire you out. What she bid me say, I will keep to myself. But first let me tell you, if you should deal double with her, truly it were an ill thing to be offered to any gentlewoman, and very weak dealing.
items.plain: My young lady asked me to find you. What she told me to say, I'll keep to myself. But first let me tell you this: if you trick her, it would be a terrible way to treat a young lady, a very low thing to do.
items.why: His friends have gone. You warn Romeo not to play games with Juliet.

lines: Nurse, commend me to thy lady and mistress.
Bid her devise
Some means to go to shrift this afternoon,
And there she shall at Friar Lawrence’ cell
Be shrived and married.
items.plain: Nurse, give my greetings to your lady. Tell her to find a way to go to confession this afternoon. There, at Friar Lawrence's cell, she'll be forgiven her sins and married.
items.why: She has come from Juliet. You give her the plan: confession this afternoon, then the wedding.

lines: This afternoon, sir? Well, she shall be there.
items.plain: This afternoon, sir? She'll be there.
items.why: The wedding is this afternoon. You promise Juliet will come.

lines: Farewell. Commend me to thy lady.
items.plain: Goodbye. Give my greetings to your lady.
items.why: It's settled. You say goodbye.

lines: Ay, a thousand times.— Boy.
items.plain: Yes, a thousand times. Boy!
items.why: He sends greetings to Juliet. You promise to pass them on and call your servant.

lines: Anon.
items.plain: Coming.
items.why: The Nurse calls again. You answer.

lines: Before and apace.
items.plain: Go ahead of me, and quickly.
items.why: Time to go. You send your servant ahead.

scenes.summary: Mercutio and Benvolio tease Romeo about disappearing last night. The Nurse arrives looking for him. Romeo gives her the plan. Juliet should come to Friar Lawrence's cell this afternoon to be married.

wants.mercutio: To joke with Romeo, and to make fun of the Nurse.
wants.benvolio: To tell Romeo that Tybalt has sent a challenge.
wants.romeo: To get the wedding plan to Juliet through the Nurse.
wants.nurse: To make sure Romeo is serious about Juliet before you pass on any message.
wants.servant-2: To do whatever the Nurse tells you.

scenes.title: Juliet Waits

lines: The clock struck nine when I did send the Nurse.
In half an hour she promised to return.
Perchance she cannot meet him. That’s not so.
Had she affections and warm youthful blood,
She would be as swift in motion as a ball;
But old folks, many feign as they were dead,
Unwieldy, slow, heavy, and pale as lead.
[Enter NURSE and SERVANT #2.]
O, honey nurse, what news?
Hast thou met with him? Send thy man away.
items.plain: The clock struck nine when I sent the Nurse. She promised to be back in half an hour. Maybe she can't find him. No, that can't be it. If she had young, warm blood, she'd move as fast as a ball. But old people act as if they were dead: clumsy, slow, heavy, and pale as lead. Oh, sweet Nurse, what's the news? Did you meet him? Send your servant away.
items.why: The Nurse has been gone three hours. You're desperate for news, and then she arrives.

lines: You, stay at the gate.
items.plain: You, wait at the gate.
items.why: Juliet wants privacy. You send your servant to the gate.

lines: Now, good sweet nurse—
items.plain: Now, good sweet Nurse...
items.why: You're alone at last. You beg for the news.

lines: I am aweary. Give me leave awhile.
Fie, how my bones ache! What a jaunt have I!
items.plain: I'm tired. Leave me alone for a minute. Oh, how my bones ache! What a trip I've had!
items.why: She's begging, but you're worn out, and you enjoy making her wait.

lines: Come, I pray thee, speak. Good, good nurse, speak.
items.plain: Come on, please, speak. Good, good Nurse, speak.
items.why: She's stalling. You plead.

lines: Do you not see that I am out of breath?
items.plain: Can't you see I'm out of breath?
items.why: She keeps pushing. You say you're out of breath.

lines: How art thou out of breath, when thou hast breath
To say to me that thou art out of breath?
Is thy news good or bad? Answer to that.
items.plain: How can you be out of breath when you have enough breath to tell me you're out of breath? Is the news good or bad? Answer that.
items.why: She says she's out of breath, while talking. You point that out.

lines: Lord, how my head aches! What a head have I!
It beats as it would fall in twenty pieces.
My back o’t’ other side! Ah, my back, my back!
Beshrew your heart for sending me about
To catch my death with jaunting up and down.
items.plain: Lord, how my head hurts! It's pounding as if it would break into twenty pieces. And my back! Oh, my back, my back! Shame on you for sending me out to catch my death running up and down.
items.why: You still won't tell. You complain about your head and your back.

lines: I’ faith, I am sorry that thou art not well.
Sweet, sweet, sweet nurse, tell me, what says my love?
items.plain: Truly, I'm sorry you don't feel well. Sweet, sweet, sweet Nurse, tell me, what does my love say?
items.why: She's in pain, and you feel bad, but you have to know.

lines: Have you got leave to go to shrift today?
items.plain: Do you have permission to go to confession today?
items.why: She's suffered enough. You start: does she have permission to go to confession?

lines: I have.
items.plain: I do.
items.why: She asks if you can go to confession. You can.

lines: Then hie you hence to Friar Lawrence’ cell.
There stays a husband to make you a wife.
Go. I’ll to dinner. Hie you to the cell.
items.plain: Then hurry to Friar Lawrence's cell. A husband is waiting there to make you a wife. Go. I'm going to lunch. Hurry to the cell.
items.why: She can go. You finally tell her: Romeo is waiting to marry her.

lines: Hie to high fortune! Honest nurse, farewell.
items.plain: I'm hurrying to my good fortune! Honest Nurse, goodbye.
items.why: It's happening. You run off to be married.

scenes.summary: Juliet waits impatiently for the Nurse to return. The Nurse teases her by complaining about her aches before finally giving the news. Romeo is waiting at the Friar's cell to marry her.

wants.juliet: To get the news out of the Nurse right now.
wants.nurse: To catch your breath, and to enjoy making Juliet wait a little.

scenes.title: The Wedding

items.text: Wedding with ROMEO, JULIET, FRIAR LAWRENCE, and NURSE.

scenes.summary: Romeo and Juliet are married in secret by Friar Lawrence. There are no spoken lines in this scene.

scenes.title: Mercutio and Tybalt

lines: I pray thee, good Mercutio, let’s retire.
The day is hot, the Capulets are abroad,
And if we meet we shall not ‘scape a brawl.
items.plain: Please, Mercutio, let's go home. It's a hot day and the Capulets are out. If we meet them, we won't be able to avoid a fight.
items.why: It's hot and the Capulets are out. You want to get Mercutio home before a fight starts.

lines: Thou art like one of these fellows that, when he enters the confines of a tavern, claps me his sword on the table and says “God send me to no need of thee”, and by the operation of the second cup, draws him on the drawer when indeed there is no need.
items.plain: You're like one of those men who walks into a tavern, slaps his sword on the table and says "I hope I never need you," and then after his second drink pulls his sword on the waiter for no reason at all.
items.why: Benvolio wants to leave. You tease him for being the real hothead.

lines: By my head, here comes the Capulets.
items.plain: I swear, here come the Capulets.
items.why: Too late. You see the Capulets coming.

lines: By my heel, I care not.
items.plain: I swear, I don't care.
items.why: Benvolio warns you. You couldn't care less.

lines: Gentleman, good e’en. A word with one of you.
items.plain: Good afternoon, gentlemen. I'd like a word with one of you.
items.why: You're hunting for Romeo. You ask his friends for a word.

lines: And but one word with one of us? Couple it with something. Make it a word and a blow.
items.plain: Just one word with one of us? Add something to it. Make it a word and a punch.
items.why: Tybalt wants "a word." You dare him to make it a fight.

lines: Mercutio, thou consortest with Romeo.
items.plain: Mercutio, you hang around with Romeo.
items.why: Mercutio is baiting you. You accuse him of being Romeo's companion.

lines: Consort? Zounds, consort!
items.plain: "Hang around"? Good grief, hang around!
items.why: He says you "consort" with Romeo. You take it as an insult.

lines: We talk here in the public haunt of men.
Either withdraw unto some private place,
Or reason coldly of your grievances,
Or else depart. Here all eyes gaze on us.
items.plain: We're talking out here in public. Either go somewhere private, or talk about your complaints calmly, or else leave. Everyone is staring at us.
items.why: This is about to explode in public. You try to move them or calm them.

lines: Men’s eyes were made to look, and let them gaze.
I will not budge for no man’s pleasure, I.
items.plain: People's eyes were made for looking, so let them stare. I won't move to please anyone.
items.why: Benvolio wants you to move. You refuse to budge for anyone.

lines: Well, peace be with you, sir. Here comes my man.
Romeo, the love I bear thee can afford
No better term than this: thou art a villain.
items.plain: Well, peace to you, sir. Here comes the man I want. Romeo, the kindest thing I can say to you is this: you are a villain.
items.why: Romeo walks in. He's the one you want, so you insult him.

lines: Tybalt, the reason that I have to love thee
Doth much excuse the appertaining rage
To such a greeting. Villain am I none.
Therefore farewell. I see thou knows me not.
items.plain: Tybalt, I have a reason to love you, and it lets me excuse the anger in that greeting. I'm no villain. So goodbye. I can see you don't know me.
items.why: Tybalt calls you a villain. You've just married his cousin, so you refuse to fight.

lines: This shall not excuse the injuries
That thou hast done me. Therefore turn and draw.
items.plain: That doesn't excuse the insults you've done to me. So turn around and draw your sword.
items.why: Romeo won't fight. You won't let him off, and order him to draw.

lines: I do protest I never injured thee
But love thee better than thou canst devise.
And so, good Capulet, which name I tender
As dearly as mine own, be satisfied.
items.plain: I swear I never insulted you. I love you more than you can understand. So, good Capulet, a name I care about as much as my own, be satisfied.
items.why: He demands a fight. You tell him, mysteriously, that you love him.

lines: O calm, dishonorable, vile submission!
Alla stoccato carries it away.
Tybalt, you ratcatcher will you walk?
items.plain: What a calm, dishonorable, disgusting way to give in! The sword fighter wins the day. Tybalt, you rat-catcher, will you fight?
items.why: Romeo is backing down. You're disgusted, and challenge Tybalt yourself.

lines: What wouldst thou have with me?
items.plain: What do you want with me?
items.why: Mercutio draws on you. You ask what he wants.

lines: Good king of cats, nothing but one of your nine lives.
items.plain: Good King of Cats, I only want one of your nine lives.
items.why: He asks what you want. One of his nine lives.

lines: I am for you.
items.plain: I'm ready for you.
items.why: Mercutio insults you. You accept the fight.

lines: Gentle Mercutio, put thy weapon up.
Draw, Benvolio, beat down their weapons.
Tybalt! Mercutio! The Prince expressly hath
Forbid this bandying in Verona streets.
Hold, Tybalt! Good Mercutio!
items.plain: Gentle Mercutio, put your sword away. Benvolio, draw and knock their swords down. Tybalt! Mercutio! The Prince has forbidden this fighting in Verona's streets. Stop, Tybalt! Good Mercutio!
items.why: Your friend and your new cousin are fighting. You try to stop them.

items.text: They fight. TYBALT stabs MERCUTIO through ROMEO’S arms. TYBALT Exits.

lines: I am hurt.
A plague o’ both houses! I am sped.
Is he gone and hath nothing?
items.plain: I'm hurt. A curse on both your families! I'm finished. Did he get away without a scratch?
items.why: Tybalt's sword got you under Romeo's arm. You realise it's serious.

lines: What, art thou hurt?
items.plain: What, are you hurt?
items.why: Mercutio says he's hurt. You can't believe it.

lines: Ay, ay, a scratch, a scratch. Marry, ’tis enough.
items.plain: Yes, yes, a scratch, a scratch. But it's enough.
items.why: Benvolio asks if you're hurt. You joke that it's only a scratch, but you know better.

lines: Courage, man, the hurt cannot be much.
items.plain: Be brave, man. The wound can't be that bad.
items.why: He says it's a scratch. You try to encourage him.

lines: Ask for me tomorrow and you shall find me a grave man. A plague o’ both your houses! Why the devil came you between us? I was hurt under your arm.
A plague o’ both your houses!
They have made worms’ meat of me.
Your houses!
items.plain: Ask for me tomorrow and you'll find me a grave man. A curse on both your families! Why the devil did you come between us? I was stabbed under your arm. A curse on both your families! They've made worm food of me. Your families!
items.why: You're dying. You blame both families, and Romeo for getting in the way.

lines: This gentleman, the Prince’s near ally,
My very friend hath got this mortal hurt
In my behalf. My reputation stained
With Tybalt’s slander—Tybalt, that an hour
Hath been my cousin!
items.plain: This gentleman, the Prince's relative and my true friend, got this deadly wound defending me. And my good name was ruined by Tybalt's insult. Tybalt, who has been my cousin for one hour!
items.why: Mercutio is carried off. You realise he was hurt because of you.

lines: O Romeo, Romeo, brave Mercutio is dead. [Enter TYBALT.]
Here comes the furious Tybalt back again.
items.plain: Oh Romeo, Romeo, brave Mercutio is dead. And here comes the furious Tybalt back again.
items.why: You come back with terrible news, and see Tybalt returning.

lines: Now, Tybalt, take the “villain” back again
That late thou gavest me, for Mercutio’s soul
Is but a little way above our heads,
Staying for thine to keep him company.
Either thou or I, or both must go with him.
items.plain: Now, Tybalt, take back the "villain" you called me. Mercutio's soul is only a little way above our heads, waiting for yours to keep him company. Either you or I, or both of us, must go with him.
items.why: Mercutio is dead and Tybalt is back. Now you want revenge.

lines: Thou, wretched boy, that didst consort him here
Shalt with him hence.
items.plain: You wretched boy, you were his friend here, and you'll go with him.
items.why: Romeo threatens you. You threaten him right back.

lines: This shall determine that.
items.plain: This sword will decide that.
items.why: No more talk. You fight.

items.text: They fight. ROMEO stabs TYBALT. TYBALT dies.

lines: Romeo, away, begone!
The citizens are up, and Tybalt slain.
Hence, be gone, away.
items.plain: Romeo, run, get away! The people are coming, and Tybalt is dead. Go, get out of here.
items.why: Tybalt is dead and people are coming. You tell Romeo to run.

lines: O, I am Fortune’s fool!
items.plain: Oh, I am fortune's fool!
items.why: You've just killed your wife's cousin. You see how fate has played you.

items.text: Enter PRINCE, LADY MONTAGUE, LORD CAPULET and LADY CAPULET.

lines: Where are the vile beginners of this fray?
items.plain: Where are the wicked people who started this fight?
items.why: You arrive to find bodies in the street. You demand to know who started it.

lines: O noble prince, I can discover all
The unlucky manage of this fatal brawl.
There lies the man, slain by young Romeo,
That slew thy kinsman, brave Mercutio.
items.plain: Noble Prince, I can tell you everything about this deadly fight. There lies the man, killed by young Romeo, who killed your relative, brave Mercutio.
items.why: The Prince asks what happened. You tell him.

lines: Romeo slew him; he slew Mercutio.
Who now the price of his dear blood doth owe?
items.plain: Romeo killed him, and he killed Mercutio. Who should pay now for Mercutio's precious blood?
items.why: Two men are dead. You ask who must pay.

lines: Not Romeo, Prince; he was Mercutio’s friend.
His fault concludes but what the law should end,
The life of Tybalt.
items.plain: Not Romeo, Prince. He was Mercutio's friend. He only did what the law would have done: he took Tybalt's life.
items.why: Your son's life is at stake. You plead for him.

lines: And for that offense
Immediately we do exile him hence.
Let Romeo hence in haste,
Else, when he is found, that hour is his last.
Bear hence this body and attend our will.
Mercy but murders, pardoning those that kill.
items.plain: And for that crime, we banish him at once. Romeo must leave quickly. If he is found here, that hour will be his last. Carry this body away and do as I say. Showing mercy to killers only leads to more killing.
items.why: You've heard both sides. You give your sentence: Romeo is banished.

scenes.summary: On a hot afternoon Tybalt comes looking for Romeo. Romeo, now secretly married to Tybalt's cousin, refuses to fight. Mercutio fights instead and is killed. Romeo kills Tybalt in revenge, and the Prince banishes him.

wants.benvolio: To keep the peace, and afterwards to tell the Prince the truth.
wants.mercutio: To stand up to Tybalt when Romeo will not.
wants.tybalt: To punish Romeo for coming to the party.
wants.romeo: To keep the peace with your new cousin, until Mercutio dies. Then you want revenge.
wants.prince: To find out who is to blame and stop the killing.

scenes.title: Terrible News

lines: Gallop apace, you fiery-footed steeds,
Towards Phoebus’ lodging. Such a wagoner
As Phaeton would whip you to the west
And bring in cloudy night immediately.
Come, night. Come, Romeo. Come, gentle night,
Give me my Romeo, and when I shall die,
Take him and cut him out in little stars,
And he will make the face of heaven so fine
That all the world will be in love with night
And pay no worship to the garish sun.
[Enter NURSE.]
O, here comes my nurse.
Ay me, what news? Why dost thou wring thy hands?
items.plain: Gallop fast, you fiery horses pulling the sun, and take it home so cloudy night comes right away. Come, night. Come, Romeo. Come, gentle night, and give me my Romeo. When I die, take him and cut him into little stars. He'll make the sky so beautiful that the whole world will fall in love with night and stop caring about the bright sun. Oh, here comes my Nurse. What's the news? Why are you wringing your hands?
items.why: You're waiting for your wedding night. You beg the sun to set, and then the Nurse comes in upset.

lines: He’s dead, he’s dead, he’s dead!
We are undone, lady, we are undone.
Alack the day, he’s gone, he’s killed, he’s dead.
items.plain: He's dead, he's dead, he's dead! We're ruined, lady, we're ruined. What an awful day. He's gone, he's killed, he's dead.
items.why: You've just seen Tybalt killed. You can hardly get the words out.

lines: Can heaven be so envious?
items.plain: Can heaven be so cruel?
items.why: She says "he's dead." You think she means Romeo.

lines: O Romeo, Romeo,
Whoever would have thought it? Romeo!
items.plain: Oh, Romeo, Romeo. Who would ever have thought it? Romeo!
items.why: You're in shock. You cry out Romeo's name.

lines: What devil art thou that dost torment me thus?
If he be slain, say “Ay” or if not, “No.”
Brief sounds determine my weal or woe.
items.plain: What kind of devil are you, to torture me like this? If he's been killed, say yes. If not, say no. Those short words decide my joy or my sorrow.
items.why: She won't say it plainly. You demand a yes or no.

lines: O Tybalt, Tybalt, the best friend I had!
O honest gentleman
That ever I should live to see thee dead!
items.plain: Oh Tybalt, Tybalt, the best friend I had! Oh, honest gentleman! I never thought I'd live to see you dead.
items.why: You're grieving for Tybalt. You wail about him.

lines: What storm is this that blows so contrary?
Is Romeo slaughtered and is Tybalt dead?
My dearest cousin, and my dearer lord?
items.plain: What storm is this, blowing from both directions? Is Romeo killed, and is Tybalt dead? My dear cousin and my even dearer husband?
items.why: Now it's Tybalt. You're confused: are both dead?

lines: Tybalt is gone and Romeo banish’ed.
Romeo that killed him—he is banish’ed.
Shame come to Romeo!
items.plain: Tybalt is dead and Romeo is banished. Romeo killed him, and he's banished. Shame on Romeo!
items.why: You finally tell her straight: Tybalt is dead, Romeo did it, and he's banished.

lines: Blistered be thy tongue
For such a wish! He was not born to shame.
Upon his brow shame is ashamed to sit.
items.plain: May your tongue get blisters for wishing that! He wasn't born for shame. Shame would be ashamed to sit on his face.
items.why: The Nurse curses Romeo. You turn on her.

lines: Will you speak well of him that killed your cousin?
items.plain: Will you say good things about the man who killed your cousin?
items.why: She defends him. You can't believe it.

lines: Shall I speak ill of him that is my husband?
Ah, poor my lord, what tongue shall smooth thy name
When I, thy three-hours wife, have mangled it?
My husband lives, that Tybalt would have slain.
And Tybalt’s dead, that would have slain my husband.
All this is comfort. Wherefore weep I then?
items.plain: Should I say bad things about my own husband? Oh, my poor husband, who will speak kindly of you when I, your wife of three hours, have spoken badly? My husband is alive, and Tybalt wanted to kill him. Tybalt is dead, and he would have killed my husband. All of that is good news. So why am I crying?
items.why: She asks how you can defend him. He's your husband. You work out that his being alive is good news.

lines: Hie to your chamber. I’ll find Romeo
To comfort you.
He is hid at Lawrence’ cell.
items.plain: Go to your room. I'll find Romeo to comfort you. He's hiding at Friar Lawrence's cell.
items.why: She's heartbroken. You offer to find Romeo for her.

scenes.summary: Juliet waits happily for her wedding night. The Nurse brings terrible news, but tells it so badly that Juliet first thinks Romeo is dead. The truth is that Romeo has killed Tybalt and been banished.

wants.juliet: To find out exactly what has happened, and then to stand by your husband.
wants.nurse: To share your grief for Tybalt, and then to comfort Juliet.

scenes.title: Banished

lines: Romeo, come forth; come forth thou fearful man.
items.plain: Romeo, come out. Come out, you frightened man.
items.why: You've come back from the Prince with news. You call Romeo out of hiding.

lines: Father, what news? What is the Prince’s doom?
items.plain: Father, what's the news? What is the Prince's punishment?
items.why: The Friar is back. You're afraid to hear your punishment.

lines: Not body’s death, but body’s banishment.
items.plain: Not death. You are banished.
items.why: He asks his sentence. You think it's good news.

lines: Ha, banishment?
items.plain: Ha, banished?
items.why: "Banishment." To you that's worse than death.

lines: Here from Verona art thou banish’ed.
Be patient, for the world is broad and wide.
items.plain: You are banished from Verona. Be patient. The world is big and wide.
items.why: He's horrified. You tell him to be patient.

lines: There is no world without Verona walls
But purgatory, torture, hell itself.
items.plain: There is no world outside Verona's walls, only suffering, torture, and hell itself.
items.why: He says the world is wide. For you there's no world without Juliet.

lines: O deadly sin, O rude thankfulness!
This is dear mercy, and thou seest it not.
items.plain: Oh, what a terrible sin! How ungrateful! This is mercy, and you can't even see it.
items.why: He's ungrateful. You scold him.

lines: ’Tis torture and not mercy. Heaven is here
Where Juliet lives, and every cat and dog
And little mouse, every unworthy thing,
Live here in heaven and may look on her,
But Romeo may not; he is banish’ed.
O friar, the damn’ed use that word in hell.
Howling attends it. How hast thou the heart
Being a divine, a ghostly confessor,
A sin absolver, and my friend professed,
To mangle me with that word “banish’ed”.
items.plain: It's torture, not mercy. Heaven is here, where Juliet lives. Every cat and dog and little mouse, every worthless thing, lives here in heaven and can look at her. But Romeo can't. He is banished. Friar, people in hell use that word, and they howl when they say it. How do you, a holy man, my confessor and my friend, have the heart to crush me with that word "banished"?
items.why: He calls it mercy. You explain why being banished from Juliet is torture.

lines: [NURSE knocks.] Arise. One knocks. Good Romeo, hide thyself.
Who knocks so hard? Whence came you? What’s your will?
items.plain: Get up. Someone's knocking. Romeo, hide yourself. Who is knocking so hard? Where are you from? What do you want?
items.why: Someone is knocking. You tell Romeo to hide, and ask who's there.

lines: I come from Lady Juliet.
items.plain: I come from Lady Juliet.
items.why: The Friar asks who you are. You say who sent you.

lines: Welcome, then.
items.plain: Welcome, then.
items.why: It's Juliet's Nurse. You let her in.

lines: O holy friar,
Where’s my lady’s lord? Where’s Romeo?
items.plain: Oh, holy Friar, where is my lady's husband? Where is Romeo?
items.why: You've come for Romeo. You ask where he is.

lines: There on the ground, with his own tears made drunk.
items.plain: There on the ground, drunk on his own tears.
items.why: She asks for Romeo. You point at him, crying on the floor.

lines: Stand up, stand up. Stand up an you be a man.
For Juliet’s sake, for her sake, rise and stand.
items.plain: Stand up, stand up. Stand up if you're a man. For Juliet's sake, get up and stand.
items.why: You see him on the ground. You tell him to get up, for Juliet's sake.

lines: Spakest thou of Juliet? How is it with her?
items.plain: Did you say Juliet? How is she?
items.why: She said "Juliet." You need to know how she is.

lines: O, she says nothing, sir, but weeps and weeps.
items.plain: Oh, she doesn't say anything, sir. She only cries and cries.
items.why: He asks about Juliet. You tell him she only cries.

lines: What, rouse thee, man! Thy Juliet is alive.
Go, get thee to thy love, as was decreed.
Hence and comfort her.
But look thou stay not till the watch be set.
Go before, nurse. Commend me to thy lady.
Romeo is coming.
items.plain: Pull yourself together, man! Your Juliet is alive. Go to your love, as we planned, and comfort her. But don't stay until the guards come on duty. Nurse, go ahead and give my greetings to your lady. Romeo is coming.
items.why: They're both falling apart. You take charge and send him to Juliet, with a warning to leave early.

lines: My lord, I’ll tell my lady you will come.
items.plain: My lord, I'll tell my lady you're coming.
items.why: The plan is set. You go to tell Juliet.

lines: Go hence, good night—
Either be gone before the watch be set
Or by the break of day disguised from hence.
Farewell. Goodnight.
items.plain: Go, good night. Either leave before the guards come on duty, or leave in disguise at dawn. Goodbye. Good night.
items.why: The Nurse has gone. You repeat the most important part: be gone before the guards.

lines: But that a joy past joy calls out on me,
It were a grief so brief to part with thee.
Farewell.
items.plain: If a joy greater than joy weren't calling me, it would be sad to leave you so quickly. Goodbye.
items.why: You have to leave the Friar. Only Juliet could pull you away so fast.

scenes.summary: Romeo hides at Friar Lawrence's cell and falls apart when he hears he is banished. The Nurse arrives. The Friar pulls Romeo together and sends him to say goodbye to Juliet before leaving for Mantua.

wants.friar-lawrence: To calm Romeo down and get him safely out of Verona.
wants.romeo: To be with Juliet. Being sent away from her feels worse than death.
wants.nurse: To find Romeo and bring him to Juliet.

scenes.title: A Wedding Is Planned

items.text: Enter CAPULET, LADY CAPULET, and PARIS.

lines: Things have fallen out, sir, so unluckily,
That we have had no time to move our daughter.
Look you, she loved her kinsman Tybalt dearly.
’Tis very late. She’ll not come down tonight.
